title: What Can a 1-Year-Old Usually Do? A Gentle At-Home Checklist
label: Development Checklists
desc: A simple look at the movement, hand, and play skills many 1-year-olds are working on, plus everyday ways to practice them.
html:
The first birthday brings a lot of questions, and the most common one is "Should my baby be walking yet?"

My wife, a pediatric occupational therapist, always says the same thing: look at the order of skills, not the exact date.

Body and movement

  • Pulls up to stand using furniture
  • Cruises, stepping sideways while holding on
  • Takes first steps (the normal range is wide, roughly 9 to 18 months)
  • Crawls, or gets around in their own way

Hands and play

  • Picks up small things with thumb and index finger
  • Bangs two toys together
  • Puts objects into a container and takes them out
  • Points to show you something interesting

Easy ways to practice

  • Put toys on the sofa so standing and cruising have a purpose
  • Offer a box and a few blocks for in-and-out play
  • Let them feed themselves soft finger foods for pincer practice

When to ask

If your child isn't bearing weight on their legs, doesn't use one hand, or has lost a skill they had, bring it up with your pediatrician.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Teaching Kids to Put On Their Own Shoes
label: Daily Routines
desc: Putting on shoes takes balance, hand strength, and body awareness. Here's an easy step-by-step way to teach it.
html:
Shoes are often the last step before leaving the house, which is exactly why kids rarely get to practice.

My wife says putting on shoes needs balance, hand strength, and a sense of where the foot is, all at once.

Step by step

  • Sit down on a low stool or the floor. Standing on one foot is too hard at first
  • Open the shoe wide and pull the tongue up
  • Push the foot in, toes first, then the heel
  • Close the strap

What helps

  • Start with Velcro shoes; laces come much later
  • Put a small stool by the door as the shoe spot
  • Cut one sticker in half and put each half inside a shoe; when the halves match, the shoes are on the right feet
  • Practice on weekends when there's no rush

Wrapping up

Let your child do the first part, and you finish. Each week, hand over one more step.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Buttoning Skills by Age: From Big Buttons to Shirt Fronts
label: Daily Routines
desc: Buttons are one of the trickiest self-care skills. Here are the stages and simple games that build the finger skills behind them.
html:
Buttons look simple to adults, but for kids they're a real puzzle: one hand pushes, the other hand pulls, and the eyes have to guide both.

My wife says unbuttoning comes first because it's easier.

Typical stages

  • Around 3: unbuttons large buttons
  • 3 to 4: buttons large buttons on the front of a coat
  • 4 to 5: manages smaller buttons
  • 5 to 6: buttons a shirt; cuffs are often the last to come

Practice games

  • Push coins into a slot in a box (same pinch-and-push motion)
  • Make a "button snake": felt squares with slits threaded onto a ribbon with a big button at the end
  • Practice on clothes laid flat on the lap first, not while wearing them
  • Start from the bottom button so the lining-up is easier to see

Wrapping up

Big buttons, lots of time, and practice on the lap make the biggest difference.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Is My Child Left-Handed? When Hand Preference Shows Up
label: Development Checklists
desc: Hand preference develops gradually. Here's when it usually settles, why switching hands is normal early on, and how to support a lefty.
html:
Parents often notice their toddler switching hands and wonder which one will "win."

My wife says it's completely normal for little ones to use both hands, and preference shows up gradually.

When it settles

  • Under 2: kids often use both hands
  • 2 to 3: a preference starts to appear
  • 4 to 6: for most kids, it's fairly clear
  • There's no need to push a child toward either hand

Helping a left-handed child

  • Use left-handed scissors, so the blades don't block the view
  • Tilt the paper slightly to the right
  • Seat them on the left side at the table so elbows don't bump
  • Encourage a grip that keeps the hand below the writing line, so they can see what they write

When to ask

If a child under 18 months strongly avoids using one hand, mention it to your pediatrician.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Throwing and Catching a Ball: What to Expect by Age
label: Development Checklists
desc: Ball skills develop in stages. Here's what throwing and catching usually look like from toddlers to kindergarten, and how to practice.
html:
Catching is surprisingly hard. The eyes track the ball, the brain predicts where it'll land, and both hands have to move together.

My wife's tip: start bigger, softer, and slower than you think.

Typical stages

  • Around 2: throws forward, any style
  • Around 3: catches a big ball against the chest with both arms
  • Around 4: catches with hands more than arms
  • Around 5: overhand throws toward a target

Practice tips

  • Use a big soft ball or even a balloon (it moves slowly)
  • Stand close, about one big step apart
  • Sit on the floor and roll the ball back and forth first
  • Throw at a target, like a laundry basket

Wrapping up

If your child flinches or turns away, go back to balloons and rolling. Confidence comes before speed.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Standing on One Foot: Balance Milestones and Easy Games
label: Development Checklists
desc: Standing on one foot is a key balance skill. Here's what's typical by age and playful ways to build it at home.
html:
Standing on one foot shows up in many development checklists because it uses core strength, leg strength, and balance together.

My wife says it also matters for everyday things like putting on pants while standing.

Typical balance by age (rough guide)

  • Around 3: one or two seconds
  • Around 4: about four to five seconds
  • Around 5: around ten seconds
  • Around 6: hops on one foot several times

Balance games

  • Flamingo contest: who can stand on one foot longest?
  • Freeze dance: when the music stops, freeze on one foot
  • Stepping stones: pillows on the floor to step across
  • Kicking a ball: the standing leg does the balance work

When to ask

If one side is much weaker than the other, or your child falls much more often than peers, talk to your pediatrician.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Play Dough by Age: Simple Ideas That Build Hand Strength
label: Sensory & Play
desc: Play dough is one of the best hand-strength tools. Here are age-by-age ideas, from squishing to making letters.
html:
If my wife had to pick one toy for hand strength, play dough would be near the top.

Squishing, rolling, and pinching all work the small muscles of the hand.

Ideas by age

  • Around 2: squish, poke, and pull it apart
  • Around 3: roll snakes and balls
  • Around 4: pinch little pieces, cut with a plastic knife
  • Around 5: shape letters and simple figures

Just a few tools

  • A small rolling pin
  • A plastic knife for cutting practice
  • Cookie cutters for pressing
  • A garlic press for dough "spaghetti" (a family favorite in many OT clinics)

For kids who hate sticky hands

Start with tools only, and keep a towel nearby. Firmer dough is less sticky than soft dough.

Wrapping up

Ten minutes of dough before writing time is a great warm-up for little hands.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: The Blanket Burrito and Other Deep Pressure Games for Calm Bodies
label: Sensory & Play
desc: Deep pressure games like the blanket burrito can help kids feel calm and organized. Here's how to play them safely.
html:
Some kids get calmer with firm, steady pressure. That's why so many love being squeezed in a big hug.

My wife often uses the "blanket burrito" game, because it turns calming pressure into play.

How to play

  • Lay a blanket on the floor and have your child lie at one edge
  • Roll them up slowly, always keeping the head and face out
  • Add "toppings" with gentle squeezes along the arms and legs
  • Unroll when your child says so; they're in charge

More deep pressure games

  • Pillow sandwich: child between two pillows, gentle press from above
  • Firm bear hugs (firm, not tight)
  • Crawling through a cushion tunnel
  • Weighted products: ask an OT before using these, as weight and time matter

Safety first

Never cover the face, stop right away if your child asks, and keep it short, a few minutes at a time.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Smell-Sensitive Kids: When Everyday Scents Feel Too Strong
label: Sensory & Play
desc: Some kids gag at food smells or refuse certain places because of scents. Here's how smell sensitivity shows up and what helps.
html:
Some kids notice smells long before adults do, and those smells can feel overwhelming.

My wife says smell sensitivity often shows up at mealtimes and in public places.

Common signs

  • Gags at food smells before even tasting
  • Avoids bathrooms because of cleaning products
  • Comments on perfume or lotion on people
  • Refuses certain places like markets or restaurants

What helps

  • Open a window while cooking strong foods
  • Switch to unscented soap and detergent where you can
  • Let your child carry a comfort item with a familiar scent
  • Introduce new food smells from a distance before bringing them close

Wrapping up

These reactions are real, not dramatic. Small, predictable steps help kids feel in control.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Visual Perception Games: Spot the Difference, Hidden Pictures, and More
label: Sensory & Play
desc: Visual perception helps kids find letters, copy shapes, and spot details. Here are simple games that build it.
html:
Visual perception is how the brain makes sense of what the eyes see.

My wife says it's behind many school skills: finding a word on a page, copying a shape, and telling similar letters apart.

What it helps with

  • Finding things on a busy page
  • Copying shapes and letters
  • Telling apart similar shapes, like b and d
  • Seeing how puzzle pieces fit

Games to try

  • Spot the difference between two pictures
  • "I spy" by color or shape
  • Hidden picture and search-and-find books
  • Copying a simple block design from a photo
  • Matching socks from the laundry pile

Wrapping up

Five minutes of looking games a day is plenty. Keep them playful, not like a test.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Kids Who Won't Drink Water: Cups, Timing, and Small Tricks
label: Picky Eating & Mealtime
desc: Many kids refuse plain water. Here are practical ideas from cup choice to timing that make drinking water easier.
html:
Juice and milk go down easily, but plain water? Not so much for many kids.

My wife says the reasons are often practical, like the cup or the timing.

Why kids skip water

  • It has no taste, so it feels boring
  • The cup is hard to drink from
  • They're too busy playing to notice thirst
  • Very cold water can feel unpleasant

Small tricks

  • Let your child choose their own water cup
  • Offer water at fixed times: after play, with meals, after coming home
  • Try a straw cup if open cups are messy
  • Drink together and say "cheers"
  • Room-temperature water is often easier than ice-cold

Wrapping up

Keep water visible and easy to reach. If you're worried about hydration, check with your pediatrician.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Mazes and Dot-to-Dots: Pencil Practice That Feels Like Play
label: Sensory & Play
desc: Mazes and dot-to-dots build pencil control, planning, and visual skills. Here's how to pick the right level.
html:
Kids who resist writing often love mazes. It's the same pencil control, just with a goal.

My wife likes mazes because they build planning too: kids have to look ahead before they move.

Pick the right level

  • Wide paths, traced with a finger first
  • Mazes with only a few turns
  • Dot-to-dots up to 10, then up to 20
  • Thinner paths as control grows

Practice tips

  • Trace with a finger first, then with a crayon or thick pencil
  • One page is enough for a session
  • Celebrate staying inside the lines, not speed
  • Let kids draw their own mazes for you to solve

Wrapping up

If the pencil keeps going outside the path, go back to wider paths. Success keeps kids coming back.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Sticker Play for Little Hands: Peeling, Placing, and Matching
label: Sensory & Play
desc: Stickers are an easy, cheap fine motor activity. Here's how to use them at different ages.
html:
Peeling a sticker takes more skill than it seems: a pinch with the fingertips, a steady other hand, and careful placement.

My wife uses stickers all the time because kids love them and they're easy to carry.

By age

  • Around 2: big stickers, with an adult lifting the edge first
  • Around 3: peels stickers on their own
  • Around 4: places a sticker on a target dot
  • Around 5: builds sticker scenes and patterns

Sticker ideas

  • Put dot stickers along a drawn line
  • Match colored dots to the same color on paper
  • Window stickers, so kids work standing up
  • Sticker charts for daily routines

Wrapping up

Bending the sticker sheet slightly makes edges easier to lift for beginners.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: A Smoother Morning Routine: Picture Steps for Daycare and School
label: Daily Routines
desc: Rushed mornings are hard on everyone. Here's how a picture routine and a few small changes make mornings calmer.
html:
Morning is often the most stressful time of day with little kids.

My wife says the trick isn't hurrying more; it's keeping the same order every day so kids know what's next.

A simple order

  • Toilet
  • Get dressed (clothes laid out the night before)
  • Breakfast in the same seat
  • Brush teeth, shoes on, grab the bag

What helps

  • A picture chart on the wall, one picture per step
  • Prepare clothes and bags the night before
  • A visual timer that shows time running out
  • Same order every day, even on rushed mornings

Wrapping up

When kids can check the chart themselves, there's less nagging and more independence.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: When Do Kids Stop Napping? Signs and How to Handle the Transition
label: Daily Routines
desc: Dropping the nap is a big change. Here are common signs, typical ages, and how to replace naps with quiet time.
html:
At some point, the nap becomes a battle, and bedtime gets later and later.

My wife says that's often a sign the nap is on its way out, though every child is different.

Signs they're ready

  • Takes a very long time to fall asleep at nap time
  • Bedtime gets much later on nap days
  • Does fine without a nap on most days
  • Many kids drop naps somewhere between 3 and 5

Quiet time instead

  • Keep a rest time at the old nap time
  • Offer calm activities: books, puzzles, audio stories
  • Dim the lights and lie down if they want
  • Move bedtime a little earlier during the transition

Wrapping up

Daycares often keep nap time, so it's okay if weekends and weekdays look different for a while.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Setting a Snack Schedule That Helps Kids Eat Better at Meals
label: Picky Eating & Mealtime
desc: Grazing all day can make kids less hungry at meals. Here's how a simple snack schedule helps.
html:
If kids snack all day, they often aren't hungry at dinner.

My wife says a simple snack schedule is one of the easiest ways to improve mealtimes.

A simple plan

  • A mid-morning snack
  • An afternoon snack after daycare or school
  • About two hours between snacks and meals
  • Water between meals, rather than juice or milk

Tips

  • Eat snacks at the table, not while walking around
  • Serve a set portion in a small bowl
  • Pair foods, like fruit with cheese or yogurt
  • Avoid using snacks as rewards or bribes

Wrapping up

Hunger is a helpful ingredient at mealtime. Protecting it makes new foods easier to try.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Why Does My Child Chew on Sleeves and Shirt Collars?
label: Sensory & Play
desc: Chewing on clothes is often a sign a child is seeking oral input. Here's why it happens and safer alternatives.
html:
Wet sleeves and chewed collars are common in some kids.

My wife says chewing often isn't a "bad habit" but a way the body seeks calming input through the mouth.

Why kids chew

  • Chewing feels steady and calming
  • It helps some kids focus while listening
  • It can increase in stressful or new places
  • Sometimes it happens without the child noticing

Safer options

  • Crunchy snacks like carrot sticks or crackers
  • Chewy foods like bagels or dried fruit (age-appropriate)
  • Drinking thick smoothies through a straw
  • Chew tools made for kids; an OT can help you pick a safe one

When to ask

If chewing is constant, damages clothes daily, or comes with other sensory concerns, an OT evaluation can help.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Thumb Sucking and Nail Biting: When to Let It Be and When to Help
label: Daily Routines
desc: Thumb sucking and nail biting are common self-soothing habits. Here's when they're normal and gentle ways to reduce them.
html:
Thumb sucking and nail biting worry many parents.

My wife says they're usually ways kids calm themselves, so the goal is to give other calming tools rather than just saying "stop."

When it's common

  • Very common in babies and toddlers
  • Often at bedtime as a way to self-soothe
  • When bored, like while watching a screen
  • During stress or new situations

Gentle help

  • Notice when it happens most and change that situation
  • Give busy hands something to do: a squeeze ball or play dough
  • Keep nails short and smooth
  • Praise small wins; shame tends to make habits stronger

When to ask

Ask your dentist about thumb sucking if it continues as permanent teeth come in, and your pediatrician if nail biting causes sore or infected skin.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: First Crayons: Chunky, Triangular, or Regular? An OT's Take
label: Sensory & Play
desc: Crayon shape matters for little hands. Here's how to choose first crayons and why broken crayons are secretly great.
html:
The first crayon is often a toddler's first tool for marking the world.

My wife says the shape of the crayon changes how kids hold it.

Crayon types

  • Chunky crayons: easy for fist grips
  • Triangular crayons: fingers naturally find a place
  • Egg-shaped crayons: fit in the palm for the youngest
  • Regular thin crayons: better a bit later

Helpful tips

  • Break crayons in half: short crayons push kids to use fingertips instead of a fist
  • Use big paper taped to the table so it doesn't slide
  • Try vertical surfaces, like an easel or paper on the wall, which encourage a good wrist position
  • Start with just three or four colors

Wrapping up

Scribbling is real work for little hands. Every mark builds toward writing.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Going Up and Down Stairs: What's Typical by Age
label: Development Checklists
desc: Stair skills develop over several years. Here's what to expect and how to practice safely.
html:
Stairs are a great test of strength and balance, and going down is harder than going up.

My wife says that's normal: down needs more control.

Typical stages

  • Around 1: crawls up stairs
  • Around 2: walks up holding a rail or hand, both feet on each step
  • Around 3: walks up with alternating feet
  • Around 4 to 5: walks down with alternating feet

Practice tips

  • Always hold a rail or an adult's hand
  • Teach young kids to go down on their bottom or backward on hands and knees
  • Practice on low playground steps
  • Keep safety gates until your child is steady

When to ask

If your child avoids stairs entirely or always leads with the same leg long after peers alternate, mention it to your pediatrician.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Pressing Too Hard or Too Light: Helping Kids With Pencil Pressure
label: Sensory & Play
desc: Some kids tear the paper, others barely leave a mark. Here's why pencil pressure varies and how to help.
html:
Some kids press so hard the paper tears; others barely leave a mark.

My wife says both come from difficulty sensing how much force the hand is using.

What you might see

  • Too hard: torn paper, a tired hand, white fingertips
  • Too light: faint, shaky lines
  • Pressure that changes a lot within a page

Practice games

  • Carbon paper: press just enough to copy the drawing
  • Drawing on foil over a soft surface: pressing too hard tears it
  • Draw the same shape "whisper soft" and "loud dark"
  • For older kids, a mechanical pencil gives feedback: the lead snaps if you press too hard

Hand strength helps too

Play dough, clothespins, and squeeze toys build the strength that makes control easier.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Kids Who Can't Wait Their Turn: Games That Teach Patience
label: Daily Routines
desc: Waiting is a skill that grows with practice. Here are games and tools that make turn-taking easier.
html:
Waiting in line or for a turn can lead to big meltdowns.

My wife says patience isn't something kids are born with; it grows with practice.

Why waiting is hard

  • Kids don't understand how long "soon" is
  • Their bodies want to move
  • There's nothing to do while waiting
  • Hunger or tiredness makes it harder

Patience games

  • Sand timers: "When the sand runs out, it's your turn"
  • Turn-taking games like dice games or building a tower one block each
  • A "waiting bag" with stickers and a small notebook for outings
  • Counting to ten together

Wrapping up

Start with very short waits and praise right away: "Thanks for waiting!"

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Sensory Bins: How to Set One Up (and Keep the Mess Under Control)
label: Sensory & Play
desc: Sensory bins invite kids to scoop, pour, and explore textures. Here's how to set one up with things you already have.
html:
A sensory bin is simply a box filled with something to touch, scoop, and pour.

My wife says it's one of the easiest ways to give kids tactile play at home.

Setup

  • A shallow storage box
  • A base like dry rice, pasta, or beans
  • Tools: scoops, cups, tongs, funnels
  • Small toys hidden inside to find

Keeping it manageable

  • Put a mat or sheet underneath
  • One rule: everything stays in the bin
  • Keep sessions short, about 10 to 15 minutes
  • Supervise closely, especially with small items and younger kids who mouth things

For touch-sensitive kids

Let them use tools first. Hands can come later, when they're ready.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Kids Who Hate Mixed Textures: Soups, Casseroles, and Mixed Dishes
label: Picky Eating & Mealtime
desc: Some kids eat foods separately but refuse them mixed. Here's why mixed textures are hard and how to bridge the gap.
html:
Some kids happily eat rice, carrots, and chicken separately, but refuse fried rice.

My wife says mixed dishes are hard because every bite is different and unpredictable.

Why mixed is hard

  • Each bite feels different
  • Unexpected lumps can surprise the mouth
  • Two textures at once, like soft and crunchy, are harder to manage
  • It's hard to see what's inside

Bridge the gap

  • Serve the parts separately on a divided plate
  • Let your child do the mixing; control makes it less scary
  • Start with simple two-food combinations
  • Use a familiar sauce or base they already like

Wrapping up

Progress might be slow, and that's okay. Keep offering without pressure.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Balance Bike or Scooter? What Each One Builds
label: Sensory & Play
desc: Balance bikes and scooters both build balance and coordination. Here's how they differ and which age fits each.
html:
Balance bikes and scooters both build balance, but they work the body differently.

My wife says either can be a great choice depending on the child.

How they compare

  • Balance bike: both legs push, the body learns to balance on two wheels, and it leads naturally to a pedal bike
  • Scooter: one leg balances while the other pushes, building single-leg strength
  • Many kids start one of these around 2 to 3, depending on size and readiness

Safety checklist

  • A helmet every time
  • The right size: on a balance bike, feet flat on the ground while seated
  • A safe place away from roads and slopes
  • An adult nearby

Wrapping up

Whichever you choose, short rides with lots of breaks build confidence best.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Bath Time Sensory Play: Simple Ideas for Calm and Fun
label: Sensory & Play
desc: Bath time is a natural sensory playground. Here are simple ideas that build hand skills and help kids relax.
html:
The bath is full of sensations: warm water, splashing, slippery toys.

My wife says this makes it a great time for play, and also a time some sensitive kids find hard.

Play ideas

  • Pouring between cups builds wrist control
  • Squeeze toys build hand strength
  • Bath crayons for drawing on tiles
  • Foam letters that stick to the wall

For a calmer bath

  • Warm, not hot; always check the temperature
  • Dim the lights for evening baths
  • Warn before pouring water: "Water on your back now"
  • A dry washcloth over the eyes helps during hair rinsing

Safety first

Never leave a child alone in the bath, even for a moment.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: What Can a 6-Year-Old Usually Do? Motor and Self-Care Checklist
label: Development Checklists
desc: A plain-language checklist of motor, hand, and self-care skills many 6-year-olds are working on.
html:
Six is a big year: many kids start school and take on more independence.

My wife made this simple checklist of skills many 6-year-olds are working on. It's a guide, not a test.

Body and movement

  • Hops on one foot several times
  • Skips with alternating feet
  • Rides a bike, often still with training wheels
  • Catches a smaller ball with hands

Hands and self-care

  • Writes their name clearly
  • Cuts out shapes along lines
  • Manages most buttons and zippers
  • Starting to tie shoes (many are still learning)

When to ask

If your child is far behind peers in several areas, or daily tasks cause a lot of frustration, an OT evaluation can give useful ideas.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Kids Who Are Afraid of Slides and Heights: Gravitational Insecurity
label: Sensory & Play
desc: Some kids feel intense fear when their feet leave the ground. Here's what gravitational insecurity looks like and how to help gently.
html:
At the playground, some kids freeze at the bottom of the slide ladder while others zoom by.

My wife says some of these kids have "gravitational insecurity," a strong fear when their feet leave the ground.

Signs to notice

  • Fear or panic when lifted or tipped back
  • Avoids even small slides
  • Goes very slowly on stairs, gripping the rail
  • Dislikes swings and moving equipment

Gentle steps

  • Start low: jumping off one step
  • Activities where feet stay touching the ground, like a rocking chair
  • Always at the child's pace; forcing makes fear stronger
  • Ride together on a parent's lap at first

When to ask

If fear keeps your child from playing with peers, an OT can help with a gradual plan.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Car Sickness in Kids: A Sensory Look and Practical Tips
label: Daily Routines
desc: Car sickness happens when the eyes and the inner ear disagree. Here are practical tips for road trips with kids.
html:
Car sickness can turn a road trip into a long day.

My wife explains that it happens when the eyes and the balance system in the inner ear send different signals.

Why it happens

  • The body feels motion, but the eyes focus on something still, like a book or screen
  • Looking down makes it worse
  • Warm, stuffy air adds to it
  • A very empty or very full stomach can make it harder

Road trip tips

  • Encourage looking far away, out the window
  • Swap screens for songs and audio stories
  • Crack a window for fresh air
  • Take breaks every one to two hours
  • Offer a light snack before leaving

When to ask

If car sickness is severe, talk to your pediatrician before long trips. Children's motion sickness medicines have age limits, so always ask first.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Toddler Biting: Why It Happens and What to Do Instead
label: Daily Routines
desc: Biting is common in toddlers. Here's why it happens and calm, practical ways to respond.
html:
Getting a call that your child bit someone at daycare is stressful.

My wife says biting is fairly common around ages 1 to 3, and knowing the reason helps reduce it.

Why toddlers bite

  • They don't have the words yet
  • Some kids seek strong input through the mouth
  • They get overexcited during play
  • Teething makes gums sore

How to respond

  • Stop it calmly and firmly: "No biting. Biting hurts."
  • Separate briefly and care for the child who was bitten
  • Teach words to use instead, like "Stop!" or "Mine!"
  • Offer safe things to chew, like crunchy snacks or chew toys

Wrapping up

Short, calm responses work better than long lectures. Watch for patterns, such as crowded play or tired afternoons.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.

title: Kids Who Throw Everything: Give Them Something They Can Throw
label: Daily Routines
desc: Throwing is a natural stage. Instead of only saying no, here's how to give kids safe throwing play.
html:
Toys, spoons, the remote: some toddlers throw everything.

My wife says throwing is a natural skill kids want to practice, so it helps to give them a "yes" option.

Why kids throw

  • Watching things fall is fun
  • Adults react strongly, which makes it interesting
  • They enjoy using their arms
  • It's a way to show frustration

Safe throwing play

  • Rolled-up socks into a laundry basket
  • Bean bags at a target
  • Balls outside, where there's space
  • A clear rule: "This is for throwing, that isn't"

When something gets thrown

Respond calmly, without a big reaction, and pick it up together. Smaller reactions make attention-seeking throwing less exciting.

Wrapping up

Throwing practice builds hand-eye coordination. Give it a place to happen.

This post shares general information, not medical advice. If you have concerns, please talk with your pediatrician or a licensed occupational therapist.
